purpose: Supplementary qualitative reference for the two validation areas (temporal patterns, graph degree distribution) that none of the four named datasets (IEEE-CIS, PaySim, BankSim, ULB) can numerically inform -- see each dataset's own reference file's `not_usable_for` list. This file is NOT one of the four canonical reference datasets named in the brief; it exists so those two report sections have *some* documented, honestly-scoped basis for a sanity check rather than either an invented number or a silently skipped section.

temporal_patterns.qualitative_expectation: Retail/digital payment volumes in essentially every published national payment-system report show pronounced intraday and weekly structure, not a flat/uniform rate: a daytime-to-evening concentration with a materially quieter overnight trough, and a weekday/weekend split that differs by payment type (P2M spend often flatter across the week than salary-linked P2P). This is a generic, extremely well-established pattern in payments literature, not a number reproduced from IEEE-CIS/PaySim/BankSim/ULB -- none of those four publish a usable hour-of-day or day-of-week histogram (see each file's applicability_notes).
temporal_patterns.source: General characteristic repeated across public payment-system volume reporting (e.g. NPCI's published UPI product statistics show intraday and weekday/weekend variation) and standard retail-transaction time-series literature. Cited as a shape expectation only -- no specific percentage is asserted or compared numerically.
temporal_patterns.used_as: A sanity check that the generated dataset's hour-of-day and day-of-week histograms are non-uniform and show a plausible trough/peak structure, not a pass/fail numeric comparison.

graph_degree_distribution.qualitative_expectation: Real-world financial/payment transaction networks are consistently reported as heavy-tailed (right-skewed, often approximately power-law-like in the upper tail): most parties have very low in/out-degree, while a small minority (large merchants, payment hubs, occasionally mule accounts) account for a disproportionate share of edges. This is a broad, repeated finding across financial-network and fraud/AML graph literature, not a number published by IEEE-CIS/PaySim/BankSim/ULB -- none of the four publish any graph or network summary at all (see each file's applicability_notes).
graph_degree_distribution.source: General finding repeated across financial-network-science and money-laundering/fraud-graph literature (e.g. discussions accompanying network-structured fraud benchmarks such as Elliptic, and graph-based fraud detection papers generally cite heavy-tailed degree distributions as the expected structure of transaction networks).
graph_degree_distribution.used_as: A sanity check that the generated graph_edges degree distribution is right-skewed with a small high-degree tail (e.g. Gini coefficient or p99/median degree ratio well above 1), not a numeric match to any specific published value.
